subject: chemistry
topicDisplay: Reactivity 1.2 & 1.4 (AHL) — energy cycles, entropy and Gibbs energy
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.

learningObjectives.title: Standard enthalpies of formation and combustion
Calculating ΔH⦵ from formation or combustion data
The Born–Haber cycle for an ionic compound
Negative ΔG means spontaneous; finding the switch-over temperature
ΔG falls to zero at equilibrium; ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K

questions.q: Which statement about the standard enthalpy change of combustion of butane, ΔH⦵c(C₄H₁₀), is correct?
options: It includes the energy supplied to ignite the butane, as well as that released.
It refers to 1 mol of butane burned, so the equation includes 6½O₂(g).
It refers to the water formed as H₂O(g), since the flame is far hotter than 100 °C.
It includes any reaction of butane with oxygen, whether CO or CO₂ forms.
optionWhy: A student who treats the activation energy as part of the enthalpy change chooses this. The energy supplied to ignite the fuel overcomes the activation energy and is returned as the products form; ΔH⦵c depends only on the reactant and product states.

ΔH⦵c is for 1 mol of the substance burned completely with all substances in their standard states: C₄H₁₀(g) + 6½O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + 5H₂O(l). For exactly 1 mol of butane, O₂ needs the fractional coefficient 6½.
A student who thinks of the conditions in the flame chooses this. A standard enthalpy change compares substances in their standard states; water is H₂O(l) under standard conditions.
A student who counts incomplete burning as combustion chooses this. ΔH⦵c refers to complete combustion, giving CO₂(g); forming CO releases less energy and would give a different value.
questions.explain: ΔH⦵c is for 1 mol of the substance burned completely with all substances in their standard states: C₄H₁₀(g) + 6½O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + 5H₂O(l). For exactly 1 mol of butane, O₂ needs the fractional coefficient 6½.

questions.q: Carbon cannot be burned to carbon monoxide without some carbon dioxide also forming, so ΔH⦵f(CO) is found indirectly. ΔH⦵c / kJ mol⁻¹: C(s, graphite) −393.5; CO(g) −283.0. What is ΔH⦵f of CO(g)?
optionWhy: ΔH⦵f(CO) is ΔH⦵ for C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g). With ΔH⦵c data, ΔH⦵ = ΣΔH⦵c(reactants) − ΣΔH⦵c(products) = −393.5 − (−283.0) = −110.5 kJ mol⁻¹. O₂ does not burn, so it contributes zero.
A student who uses products − reactants, the order for ΔH⦵f data, gets −283.0 − (−393.5) = +110.5 kJ mol⁻¹. With ΔH⦵c data the order is reactants − products.
A student who sets ΔH⦵c of the element carbon to zero gets 0 − (−283.0) = +283.0 kJ mol⁻¹. 'Elements are zero' applies to ΔH⦵f only; carbon burns, and ΔH⦵c(C) = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹.

A student who adds both combustion values, following the CO combustion arrow backwards without changing its sign, gets −393.5 + (−283.0) = −676.5 kJ mol⁻¹. Going from CO₂ back to CO reverses the combustion of CO, contributing +283.0 kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.explain: ΔH⦵f(CO) is ΔH⦵ for C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g). With ΔH⦵c data, ΔH⦵ = ΣΔH⦵c(reactants) − ΣΔH⦵c(products) = −393.5 − (−283.0) = −110.5 kJ mol⁻¹. O₂ does not burn, so it contributes zero.
questions.working: Target: C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g). ΔH⦵ = ΣΔH⦵c(reactants) − ΣΔH⦵c(products) = [ΔH⦵c(C) + ½ × 0] − ΔH⦵c(CO) = −393.5 − (−283.0) = −110.5 kJ mol⁻¹. Cycle: C + O₂ → CO₂ (−393.5) equals C + ½O₂ → CO (ΔH⦵f) followed by CO + ½O₂ → CO₂ (−283.0), so ΔH⦵f = −393.5 + 283.0.

questions.q: Magnesium oxide, MgO(s), has ΔH⦵f = −602 kJ mol⁻¹. Which statement explains why the formation of MgO(s) from its elements is exothermic?
options: The lattice enthalpy of MgO is so large that more energy is released as the gaseous ions form the solid than is absorbed in forming them.
Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ each gain a stable full outer shell of electrons, and reaching this arrangement is what releases the energy.
Each Mg²⁺ ion bonds only to the O²⁻ ion that took its electrons, and forming that one ionic bond releases the energy.
Breaking the O=O bond when oxygen is atomized releases energy, which outweighs the energy absorbed in ionizing Mg.
optionWhy: Forming Mg²⁺(g) and O²⁻(g) from the elements is strongly endothermic overall. The small, doubly charged ions attract all their neighbours strongly, so the lattice enthalpy is very large; the energy released when the gaseous ions form the solid exceeds the energy absorbed, making ΔH⦵f negative.

A student who credits the octet with releasing energy chooses this. Forming these ions absorbs energy: Mg(g) → Mg²⁺(g) needs IE1 + IE2 = +2189 kJ mol⁻¹, and O(g) → O²⁻(g) is endothermic overall because the second electron affinity is endothermic. The energy comes from the gaseous ions forming the lattice.

A student who pictures an ionic bond between electron-transfer partners chooses this. In the lattice each ion attracts several oppositely charged neighbours, and it is these attractions summed over the whole lattice that release the energy.
A student who thinks bond breaking releases energy chooses this. Atomizing oxygen absorbs energy (half the O=O bond enthalpy), adding to the endothermic steps rather than offsetting them.
questions.explain: Forming Mg²⁺(g) and O²⁻(g) from the elements is strongly endothermic overall. The small, doubly charged ions attract all their neighbours strongly, so the lattice enthalpy is very large; the energy released when the gaseous ions form the solid exceeds the energy absorbed, making ΔH⦵f negative.

questions.q:
Nitrogen and hydrogen react to form ammonia:
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g)
Standard entropies: S⦵(N₂(g)) = 191.6 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, S⦵(H₂(g)) = 130.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, S⦵(NH₃(g)) = 192.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
What is the standard entropy change, ΔS⦵, for the reaction?
optionWhy: A student who takes S⦵ of the elements N₂ and H₂ as zero, as for ΔH⦵f, uses only the product: 2(192.8) = +385.6. Standard entropies are absolute values; N₂(g) and H₂(g) have positive S⦵ values that must be included.
A student who subtracts products from reactants gets 583.7 − 385.6 = +198.1. ΔS⦵ is products minus reactants, and a reaction that reduces the moles of gas from 4 to 2 must have a negative ΔS⦵.
A student who adds each S⦵ value once, ignoring the coefficients, gets 192.8 − (191.6 + 130.7) = −129.5. S⦵ values are per mole: 3 mol of H₂ and 2 mol of NH₃ appear in the equation.
ΔS⦵ = ΣS⦵(products) − ΣS⦵(reactants) = 2(192.8) − [191.6 + 3(130.7)] = 385.6 − 583.7 = −198.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. The negative sign agrees with the prediction: 4 mol of gas become 2 mol of gas.
questions.explain: ΔS⦵ = ΣS⦵(products) − ΣS⦵(reactants) = 2(192.8) − [191.6 + 3(130.7)] = 385.6 − 583.7 = −198.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. The negative sign agrees with the prediction: 4 mol of gas become 2 mol of gas.

questions.q: For the reaction 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g) at 150 °C, ΔG⦵ = −52.2 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = −146.6 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH⦵ for the reaction?
optionWhy: A student who substitutes the Celsius temperature gets −52.2 + 150(−0.1466) = −74.2 kJ mol⁻¹. T must be the absolute temperature, 423 K.
T = 150 + 273 = 423 K and ΔS⦵ = −0.1466 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Rearranging ΔG⦵ = ΔH⦵ − TΔS⦵ gives ΔH⦵ = ΔG⦵ + TΔS⦵ = −52.2 + 423(−0.1466) = −52.2 − 62.0 = −114.2 kJ mol⁻¹.
A student who moves the TΔS⦵ term across the equals sign without changing its sign writes ΔH⦵ = ΔG⦵ − TΔS⦵ = −52.2 + 62.0 = +9.8 kJ mol⁻¹. From ΔG⦵ = ΔH⦵ − TΔS⦵, ΔH⦵ = ΔG⦵ + TΔS⦵.
A student who uses ΔS⦵ in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ with ΔG⦵ in kJ mol⁻¹ gets −52.2 + 423(−146.6) = −62064.0. ΔS⦵ must be converted to −0.1466 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ first.
questions.explain: T = 150 + 273 = 423 K and ΔS⦵ = −0.1466 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Rearranging ΔG⦵ = ΔH⦵ − TΔS⦵ gives ΔH⦵ = ΔG⦵ + TΔS⦵ = −52.2 + 423(−0.1466) = −52.2 − 62.0 = −114.2 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.q:
Silicon is manufactured by heating silica with carbon:
SiO₂(s) + 2C(s) → Si(s) + 2CO(g)   ΔH⦵ = +690 kJ mol⁻¹
Standard entropies in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: SiO₂(s) 41.5, C(s) 5.7, Si(s) 18.8, CO(g) 197.7.
Assuming ΔH⦵ and ΔS⦵ do not change with temperature and ignoring any changes of state, above what temperature does the reaction become spontaneous?
optionWhy: A student who takes S⦵ of the elements C(s) and Si(s) as zero gets ΔS⦵ = 2(197.7) − 41.5 = +353.9 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and T = 690 000/353.9 = 1950 K. Elements have positive standard entropies, which must be included.

A student who adds each S⦵ value once, ignoring the coefficients, gets ΔS⦵ = 18.8 + 197.7 − 41.5 − 5.7 = +169.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and T = 690 000/169.3 = 4076 K. The equation shows 2 mol of C and 2 mol of CO.

ΔS⦵ = [18.8 + 2(197.7)] − [41.5 + 2(5.7)] = 414.2 − 52.9 = +361.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = +0.3613 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. ΔG⦵ = 0 when T = ΔH⦵/ΔS⦵ = 690/0.3613 = 1910 K. Both ΔH⦵ and ΔS⦵ are positive, so ΔG⦵ is negative above this temperature. (In practice silicon melts at 1687 K, so the product forms as a liquid; the calculation ignores this change of state.)
A student who divides ΔH⦵ in kJ mol⁻¹ by ΔS⦵ in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ gets 690/361.3 = 1.91 K. The units must match: 690 000 J mol⁻¹ ÷ 361.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 1910 K.
questions.explain: ΔS⦵ = [18.8 + 2(197.7)] − [41.5 + 2(5.7)] = 414.2 − 52.9 = +361.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = +0.3613 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. ΔG⦵ = 0 when T = ΔH⦵/ΔS⦵ = 690/0.3613 = 1910 K. Both ΔH⦵ and ΔS⦵ are positive, so ΔG⦵ is negative above this temperature. (In practice silicon melts at 1687 K, so the product forms as a liquid; the calculation ignores this change of state.)
questions.working: ΔS⦵ = ΣS⦵(products) − ΣS⦵(reactants) = [18.8 + 2(197.7)] − [41.5 + 2(5.7)] = 414.2 − 52.9 = +361.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. At the temperature where the reaction becomes spontaneous, ΔG⦵ = 0, so T = ΔH⦵/ΔS⦵ = (690 000 J mol⁻¹)/(361.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) = 1910 K (to the nearest kelvin). Above 1910 K, TΔS⦵ > ΔH⦵ and ΔG⦵ < 0.

questions.q: For the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g), ΔH⦵ = −197.8 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = −188.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Which statement about the reaction at 298 K is correct?
options: Not spontaneous: the entropy of the system falls in this reaction.
Spontaneous: an exothermic reaction is spontaneous whatever its ΔS⦵.
Not spontaneous: ΔG⦵ = −197.8 − 298(−188.0), which is positive.
Spontaneous: the surroundings gain more entropy than the system loses.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the system's entropy must increase for a change to be spontaneous picks this. ΔG takes into account the entropy change of the surroundings as well; here the heat released increases the entropy of the surroundings by much more than the system loses.

A student who thinks the sign of ΔH⦵ alone decides spontaneity picks this. The conclusion is right at 298 K but the reason is false: with ΔS⦵ negative, the reaction stops being spontaneous above T = ΔH⦵/ΔS⦵ ≈ 1050 K.
A student who substitutes ΔS⦵ in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ with ΔH⦵ in kJ mol⁻¹ gets a large positive value. Converted consistently, ΔG⦵ = −197.8 − 298(−0.1880) = −141.8 kJ mol⁻¹, which is negative.

The heat released raises the entropy of the surroundings by −ΔH⦵/T = 197 800/298 = +664 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, far more than the system loses (188.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). Equivalently, ΔG⦵ = −197.8 − 298(−0.1880) = −141.8 kJ mol⁻¹, which is negative.
questions.explain: The heat released raises the entropy of the surroundings by −ΔH⦵/T = 197 800/298 = +664 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, far more than the system loses (188.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). Equivalently, ΔG⦵ = −197.8 − 298(−0.1880) = −141.8 kJ mol⁻¹, which is negative.

questions.q: For the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) at 450 °C, ΔG⦵ = −61.9 kJ mol⁻¹. In a particular mixture of the three gases at this temperature, [SO₂] = 0.500 mol dm⁻³, [O₂] = 0.250 mol dm⁻³ and [SO₃] = 0.00250 mol dm⁻³. What is ΔG for the reaction in this mixture? (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
optionWhy: A student who calculates Q = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ correctly but uses log₁₀ in place of ln gets −61.9 + 6.008 × (−4.00) = −85.9 kJ mol⁻¹. The equation uses the natural logarithm: ln(1.0 × 10⁻⁴) = −9.21.
A student who adds RT ln Q in J mol⁻¹ to ΔG⦵ in kJ mol⁻¹ gets −61.9 + (−55 336.9) = −55398.8. With Q = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴, RT ln Q must be converted to −55.3 kJ mol⁻¹ before it is added.

T = 450 + 273 = 723 K and Q = (0.0025)²/((0.50)²(0.25)) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴. RT = 8.31 × 723 = 6008 J mol⁻¹ = 6.008 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔG = ΔG⦵ + RT ln Q = −61.9 + 6.008 × ln(1.0 × 10⁻⁴) = −61.9 + 6.008(−9.210) = −61.9 − 55.3 = −117.2 kJ mol⁻¹. Because Q is less than 1, RT ln Q is negative and ΔG is more negative than ΔG⦵; because Q is far below K (about 3 × 10⁴ at 723 K), ΔG is negative and the forward reaction proceeds.

A student who writes Q the wrong way up, as [SO₂]²[O₂]/[SO₃]², gets Q = 1.0 × 10⁴ and ΔG = −61.9 + 6.008 × 9.210 = −61.9 + 55.3 = −6.6 kJ mol⁻¹. For the reaction as written, Q = [SO₃]²/([SO₂]²[O₂]) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴.
questions.explain: T = 450 + 273 = 723 K and Q = (0.0025)²/((0.50)²(0.25)) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴. RT = 8.31 × 723 = 6008 J mol⁻¹ = 6.008 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔG = ΔG⦵ + RT ln Q = −61.9 + 6.008 × ln(1.0 × 10⁻⁴) = −61.9 + 6.008(−9.210) = −61.9 − 55.3 = −117.2 kJ mol⁻¹. Because Q is less than 1, RT ln Q is negative and ΔG is more negative than ΔG⦵; because Q is far below K (about 3 × 10⁴ at 723 K), ΔG is negative and the forward reaction proceeds.

questions.q: For the decomposition of ammonia, 2NH₃(g) ⇌ N₂(g) + 3H₂(g), ΔG⦵ = +32.9 kJ mol⁻¹ at 25 °C. What is the value of the equilibrium constant, K, for this reaction at 25 °C? (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
optionWhy: A student who drops the minus sign and uses ln K = ΔG⦵/RT gets ln K = +13.29 and K = e^13.29 = 5.9 × 10⁵. From ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K, ln K = −ΔG⦵/RT, which is negative when ΔG⦵ is positive, so K < 1.
A student who treats the logarithm as log₁₀ takes −13.29 as log₁₀ K and gets K = 10^−13.29 = 5.2 × 10⁻¹⁴. The equation uses the natural logarithm, so K = e^−13.29 = 1.7 × 10⁻⁶.
A student who substitutes the Celsius temperature gets ln K = −32 900/(8.31 × 25) = −158.4 and K = e^−158.4 = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶⁹. T must be the absolute temperature, 298 K.
T = 298 K. ln K = −ΔG⦵/RT = −32 900/(8.31 × 298) = −13.29, so K = e^−13.29 = 1.7 × 10⁻⁶. A positive ΔG⦵ gives a negative ln K and K < 1: at 298 K the reactant, ammonia, is favoured at equilibrium.
questions.explain: T = 298 K. ln K = −ΔG⦵/RT = −32 900/(8.31 × 298) = −13.29, so K = e^−13.29 = 1.7 × 10⁻⁶. A positive ΔG⦵ gives a negative ln K and K < 1: at 298 K the reactant, ammonia, is favoured at equilibrium.
